mainEntity.name: How long does it take to get used to a new upper denture?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most people find that the initial sensations — including the feeling of bulkiness, increased saliva, and difficulty with speech or eating — begin to settle within two to four weeks of consistent daily wear. For some individuals, particularly those receiving their first denture, the full adjustment period may extend to two or three months. Wearing the denture regularly rather than removing it frequently is one of the most effective ways to shorten the adaptation period. If discomfort persists beyond this timeframe, a review appointment with your dental team is recommended to check the fit and comfort of the appliance.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel like gagging with a new upper denture?

acceptedAnswer.text: A mild gag reflex when first wearing a new upper denture is not uncommon, particularly if the posterior edge of the denture — the area near the back of the palate — feels unfamiliar. This often settles as the mouth adapts. However, a persistent or severe gag reflex that does not improve may indicate that the posterior border of the denture requires adjustment. Your dental team can assess whether the border extension is clinically appropriate for your anatomy and make any modifications needed to improve tolerance.

mainEntity.name: Why does my new denture make me sound different when I speak?

acceptedAnswer.text: Speech changes after receiving a new denture are very common and are caused by the tongue, lips, and other oral structures adjusting to the new dimensions and shape of the denture. Sounds such as "s," "f," and "th" may feel different at first. Practising speech by reading aloud, speaking slowly, and repeating challenging words is an effective way to accelerate the adaptation. Most people find their speech returns to its natural pattern within a few weeks, although the timeframe varies. If speech difficulties persist, your dental team can review the denture for any structural features that may be contributing.

mainEntity.name: Can a denture be made without a palate plate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Conventional upper complete dentures require palatal coverage to achieve suction and retention. Without the palate plate, the denture would have insufficient grip to remain stable during eating and speaking. However, in certain clinical circumstances — such as when implants are used to anchor the denture or when a patient retains some natural teeth — a horseshoe or reduced-coverage design may be considered. Whether this is clinically appropriate depends entirely on individual factors including bone structure, tissue health, and implant suitability, and can only be determined following a thorough dental assessment.

mainEntity.name: When should I return to the dentist after getting a new denture?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your dental team will typically schedule a review appointment within the first one to two weeks of receiving a new denture. This appointment allows the clinician to assess how your tissues are responding, identify any pressure points, and make any minor adjustments to improve comfort and fit. It is important to attend this appointment even if you feel the denture is comfortable. Beyond the initial review, you should contact your dental team if you experience persistent soreness, ulceration, difficulty eating, significant speech problems, or concerns about the denture's fit or stability.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my new denture causes soreness on the roof of my mouth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild, intermittent soreness in the early days of wearing a new denture can be a normal part of the adjustment period. However, if you develop persistent sore spots, ulcers, or significant discomfort on the palate or gum tissues, you should contact your dental team to arrange a review. The dentist can identify any pressure points and make targeted adjustments to relieve the areas of concern. Avoid attempting to adjust the denture yourself, as this can cause damage to the appliance or worsen discomfort. Rinsing with warm salt water may help soothe mild tissue irritation in the short term whilst awaiting a review.
